papers.title: Heredity and DNA
papers.hub: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/01 Heredity and DNA/Heredity and DNA

questions.stem: Griffith injected mice with different preparations of Streptococcus pneumoniae.

parts.stem: Which injection killed the mouse and gave living type IIIS bacteria in its tissue?
options: Live IIR mixed with heat-killed IIIS
Heat-killed IIR mixed with heat-killed IIIS
parts.explain: Something from the dead virulent IIIS cells transformed the living harmless IIR cells into virulent IIIS: the transforming principle.

questions.stem: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty set out to identify Griffith's transforming principle.

parts.stem: Describe their experiment and explain how it showed that the transforming principle is DNA.

scheme.text: IIIS extract or filtrate split into batches, each treated with a different enzyme
DNase-treated extract did not transform IIR cells
RNase- and protease-treated extracts still transformed
kw: still|occur|did transform|transformation (still )?happen|continued|not stop|no effect|did not prevent|didn.t stop|unaffected

scheme.text: So, by elimination, DNA is the transforming principle

parts.model: The IIIS extract was split into batches treated with DNase, RNase or protease, then each was mixed with live IIR cells. Only the DNase-treated batch failed to transform; RNase and protease treatment did not stop transformation. Destroying DNA alone abolished transformation, so DNA is the transforming principle.

questions.stem: Hershey and Chase grew T2 bacteriophage with ³²P or with ³⁵S, infected unlabelled E. coli, blended the cultures and centrifuged them.

parts.stem: Explain why ³²P and ³⁵S were chosen.

scheme.text: ³²P labels DNA because DNA contains phosphorus (in its backbone) and protein does not
³⁵S labels protein because protein contains sulfur (cysteine, methionine) and DNA does not

parts.model: DNA contains phosphorus but no sulfur, so ³²P labels only DNA. Protein contains sulfur (in cysteine and methionine) but no phosphorus, so ³⁵S labels only protein.

parts.stem: Where was each isotope found after centrifugation?

scheme.text: ³²P in the pellet, inside the bacteria
³⁵S in the supernatant, with the empty phage coats outside the cells

parts.model: ³²P (DNA) was in the pellet, inside the bacteria. ³⁵S (protein) stayed in the supernatant with the empty phage coats.

parts.stem: What did they conclude?

scheme.text: DNA (not protein) enters the cell, so DNA is the genetic material

parts.model: DNA, not protein, enters the bacterium and directs new phage, so DNA is the genetic material.

questions.stem: Mendel crossed tall (LeLe) and dwarf (lele) peas. The F1 were all tall. Self-fertilising the F1 gave 787 tall and 277 dwarf F2 plants.

parts.stem: Calculate the F2 ratio of tall to dwarf, as x : 1 (to 2 decimal places).
Explain the 3 : 1 ratio in terms of alleles and meiosis.

scheme.text: F1 plants are heterozygous, Lele
The alleles segregate during meiosis, so half the gametes carry Le and half carry le
Random fertilisation gives 1 LeLe : 2 Lele : 1 lele; Le is dominant so 3 tall : 1 dwarf

parts.model: The F1 are all Lele. During meiosis the two alleles segregate, so each F1 plant makes Le and le gametes in equal numbers. Random fertilisation gives 1 LeLe : 2 Lele : 1 lele. Le is dominant, so three quarters are tall and one quarter dwarf: 3 : 1.

questions.stem: The diagram shows an Agrobacterium tumefaciens cell.

parts.stem: Name the labelled structures.
Explain how Agrobacterium causes crown gall disease.

scheme.text: The T-DNA from the Ti plasmid is transferred into the plant cell and inserted into its genome
It reprograms the plant cells to grow and divide, forming a tumour (gall)

parts.model: Its vir genes transfer the T-DNA segment of the Ti plasmid into the plant cell, where it inserts into the plant genome and makes the cells proliferate into a tumour, the crown gall.

questions.stem: In the lab, E. coli can be made competent and transformed with a plasmid.

parts.stem: Explain the roles of calcium chloride and the heat shock.

scheme.text: Ca²⁺ ions neutralise the negative charges on the membrane and on the DNA phosphate backbone
This reduces repulsion so DNA can approach and bind the cell surface
A brief heat shock (42 °C) helps the plasmid cross into the cell

parts.model: Calcium ions neutralise the negative charges on the cell membrane and on DNA's phosphate backbone, reducing repulsion so the DNA can approach the cell. A brief heat shock at 42 °C then helps the plasmid cross the membrane into the cell.

questions.stem: Double-stranded DNA is heated slowly while its absorbance at 260 nm is measured.

parts.stem: Why do nucleic acids absorb UV light most strongly at 260 nm?
parts.explain: Absorption at 260 nm comes from the bases.

parts.stem: Describe and explain what happens to the absorbance as the DNA melts, and how GC content affects the melting temperature (Tm).

scheme.text: Absorbance at 260 nm increases as the DNA denatures (hyperchromic effect)
Because single-stranded, unstacked bases absorb more UV than stacked bases in the double helix
Tm is the temperature at which half of the DNA is denatured
More G–C raises Tm, because G–C pairs have three hydrogen bonds and A–T pairs two

parts.model: As the strands separate, absorbance at 260 nm rises (the hyperchromic effect), because unstacked single-stranded bases absorb more UV than bases stacked in the helix. Tm is the temperature at which half the DNA is denatured. DNA richer in G–C has a higher Tm, because each G–C pair has three hydrogen bonds against two for A–T.

questions.stem: The pea Le gene encodes gibberellin 3β-hydroxylase.

parts.stem: Explain how a single change in the DNA makes le plants dwarf.

scheme.text: An A→G substitution changes one amino acid (Ala229→Thr, A229T)
The enzyme (gibberellin 3β-hydroxylase) barely works
So little active gibberellin (GA1) is made, so less stem growth

parts.model: An A→G change swaps alanine 229 for threonine. The altered gibberellin 3β-hydroxylase has very little activity, so little active gibberellin (GA1) is made, and without this growth hormone the stem stays short.

questions.stem: Sperm tsRNAs from male mice fed a high-fat diet were injected into normal zygotes.

parts.stem: What did this show about inheritance?

scheme.text: Offspring developed metabolic disorders (glucose and insulin intolerance)
Information can be inherited without any change in DNA sequence (via RNA in sperm)

parts.model: The offspring developed glucose and insulin intolerance even though their DNA was normal: a father's diet can be passed on through RNA fragments in sperm, without any change in DNA sequence.

questions.stem: Extended answer.

parts.stem: Describe the experimental evidence that established DNA, rather than protein, as the hereditary material. Refer to at least two separate experiments.

scheme.text: Griffith: heat-killed IIIS + live IIR killed mice; living IIIS recovered (a transforming principle)
Avery, MacLeod and McCarty treated IIIS extract with different enzymes
Only DNase abolished transformation
RNase and protease did not, so DNA is the transforming principle
Hershey and Chase labelled T2 phage DNA with ³²P and protein with ³⁵S
After blending and centrifugation, ³²P was in the pellet (inside the bacteria)
³⁵S stayed in the supernatant with the phage coats
So DNA enters the cell and directs new phage; DNA, not protein, is the genetic material

parts.model: Griffith (1928) found that heat-killed virulent IIIS pneumococci mixed with live harmless IIR killed mice, and living IIIS were recovered: a transforming principle passed from dead to living cells. Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1944) treated IIIS extract with DNase, RNase or protease. Only DNase abolished transformation; RNase and protease had no effect, so the transforming principle is DNA. Hershey and Chase (1952) labelled T2 phage DNA with ³²P and protein with ³⁵S, infected E. coli, blended and centrifuged. ³²P was found in the pellet with the bacteria, while ³⁵S stayed in the supernatant with the empty coats, so only DNA entered the cell to direct new phage. DNA, not protein, is the hereditary material.

papers.title: Structure of DNA and RNA
papers.hub: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/02 Structure of DNA and RNA/Structure of DNA and RNA

questions.stem: The diagram shows a nucleotide.

parts.stem: Name the labelled parts.
State the chemical difference between ribose and deoxyribose, and which nucleic acid each is found in.

scheme.text: Ribose has an OH on the 2′ carbon; deoxyribose has only H there
Ribose is in RNA, deoxyribose in DNA

parts.model: Ribose carries an OH group on its 2′ carbon, where deoxyribose has just an H. Ribose is the sugar of RNA, deoxyribose of DNA.

questions.stem: Bases are either purines or pyrimidines.

parts.stem: Which pair are both purines?
parts.explain: Purines (adenine, guanine) have two fused rings; pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil) have one.

parts.stem: Explain why a purine always pairs with a pyrimidine in the double helix.

scheme.text: Purines have two rings and pyrimidines one, so a purine + pyrimidine pair has a constant width
Specific hydrogen bonding: A pairs with T (2 bonds), G with C (3 bonds)

parts.model: A purine (two rings) opposite a pyrimidine (one ring) keeps the helix a constant 2 nm wide, and hydrogen bonding is only right for A–T (two bonds) and G–C (three bonds).

questions.stem: Chargaff measured the base composition of DNA from different species (molar %).

parts.stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA is 30% adenine. What percentage is guanine?
State Chargaff's rule and explain how it supports the double-helix model.

scheme.text: %A = %T and %G = %C in any species
The ratio of A+T to G+C varies between species
Because A pairs with T and G with C (complementary base pairing) across the two strands

parts.model: In any double-stranded DNA, %A = %T and %G = %C, although the A+T : G+C ratio varies between species. Equal amounts are exactly what you expect if every A on one strand pairs with a T on the other and every G with a C.

questions.stem: Nucleotides in a strand are joined by phosphodiester bonds.

parts.stem: Describe a phosphodiester bond and explain how it gives a strand direction.

scheme.text: A phosphate links the 3′ carbon (3′-OH) of one sugar to the 5′ carbon of the next
It is a covalent bond in the sugar–phosphate backbone
Each strand has a free 5′ phosphate end and a free 3′-OH end, so it runs 5′→3′

parts.model: A phosphate group bridges the 3′ carbon of one sugar and the 5′ carbon of the next, forming the covalent sugar–phosphate backbone. One end of a strand has a free 5′ phosphate and the other a free 3′-OH, giving the strand a 5′→3′ direction.

parts.stem: Write the strand complementary to 5′-ATGCTTAG-3′, reading 5′ to 3′.
parts.model: 5′-CTAAGCAT-3′
parts.note: TACGAATC has the right bases but is written 3′→5′: half marks.

questions.stem: Watson and Crick's model of B-DNA drew on Franklin's X-ray diffraction images.

parts.stem: Fill in the dimensions and features.
Describe four structural features of the B-DNA double helix.

scheme.text: Two antiparallel strands
Sugar–phosphate backbone on the outside, bases on the inside
Complementary base pairs held by hydrogen bonds (A–T two, G–C three)
Right-handed helix about 2 nm wide, about 10 bp (3.4 nm) per turn, 0.34 nm per bp
Major and minor grooves

parts.model: Two antiparallel strands wind into a right-handed helix about 2 nm wide, with about 10 base pairs (3.4 nm) per turn. The sugar–phosphate backbones are on the outside and the bases stack inside, paired A–T (two hydrogen bonds) and G–C (three). The twisting creates major and minor grooves.

questions.stem: Three main types of RNA take part in gene expression.

parts.stem: Name the three main types of RNA and give the role of each.

scheme.text: mRNA carries the genetic message (copy of the gene) to the ribosome
tRNA brings amino acids to the ribosome and reads codons with its anticodon
rRNA forms the ribosome (structure and catalysis)

parts.model: mRNA carries a copy of the gene's sequence to the ribosome; tRNA delivers amino acids, matching codons with its anticodon; rRNA is the structural and catalytic core of the ribosome.

parts.stem: According to the central dogma, which transfer of sequence information never happens?
parts.explain: Information can flow between nucleic acids and from nucleic acid to protein, but never back out of protein (Crick, 1970).

questions.stem: Extended answer.

parts.stem: Explain how the structure of DNA relates to its function as the molecule of heredity. Refer to base pairing, strand directionality, and the semiconservative model of replication.

scheme.text: Information is stored in the sequence of the four bases
Complementary base pairing: A–T and G–C, by hydrogen bonds
So each strand can act as a template for an accurate copy
Hydrogen bonds are weak, so the strands can separate for copying, while the covalent backbone keeps the sequence stable
The strands are antiparallel, each with a 5′ and a 3′ end
Polymerase only adds to the 3′ end (5′→3′), giving leading and lagging strands
Semiconservative: each new molecule keeps one parental strand and one new strand
Shown by Meselson and Stahl (¹⁵N/¹⁴N), so genetic information is passed on faithfully

parts.model: Genetic information is stored in the sequence of four bases. Bases pair specifically, A with T and G with C, through hydrogen bonds, so each strand carries the information to rebuild its partner: it can act as a template. The hydrogen bonds are weak enough for the strands to separate for copying, while the covalent sugar–phosphate backbone keeps the sequence stable. The strands are antiparallel, and polymerase only adds nucleotides to a 3′ end, so one new strand is made continuously (leading) and the other in Okazaki fragments (lagging). Replication is semiconservative: each daughter molecule has one parental and one new strand, as Meselson and Stahl showed with ¹⁵N and ¹⁴N, so the sequence is copied faithfully to each daughter cell.

papers.title: DNA Replication
papers.hub: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/03 DNA Replication/DNA Replication

questions.stem: Meselson and Stahl grew E. coli for many generations in ¹⁵N medium, moved them to ¹⁴N medium, and separated the DNA by density-gradient centrifugation after each round of replication.

parts.stem: Why was the DNA first labelled with ¹⁵N and then grown in ¹⁴N?

scheme.text: ¹⁵N is a heavy isotope incorporated into the bases, making the parental DNA denser
So old (heavy) and new (light) strands can be told apart by density

parts.model: ¹⁵N is built into the bases, so parental DNA is heavy. After the switch, new strands are made with ¹⁴N and are light, so old and new DNA can be told apart by density.

parts.stem: Predict the bands after one round of replication in ¹⁴N for the conservative, semiconservative and dispersive models.

scheme.text: Conservative: two bands, one heavy and one light
Semiconservative: one intermediate band
Dispersive: one intermediate band

parts.model: Conservative: one heavy and one light band. Semiconservative: one intermediate band. Dispersive: one intermediate band.

parts.stem: After two rounds they saw one intermediate band and one light band. Which model does this support, and why does it rule out the dispersive model?

scheme.text: Semiconservative
Dispersive would give a single band (lighter than intermediate), not two separate bands

parts.model: Semiconservative replication. Dispersive replication would give a single band between intermediate and light, never a separate light band.

questions.stem: DNA polymerases cannot start a new strand on their own.

parts.stem: Explain why a primer is needed and how it is made.

scheme.text: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to an existing free 3′-OH; it cannot start a chain
Primase makes a short RNA primer (10–12 nt in E. coli)

parts.model: DNA polymerase can only extend an existing free 3′-OH, so it cannot start a strand from scratch. Primase lays down a short RNA primer (10 to 12 nucleotides in E. coli) to give it that 3′ end.

parts.stem: Describe how DNA polymerase adds a nucleotide to the growing strand.

scheme.text: The incoming dNTP pairs with the complementary base on the template
Its 5′ phosphate joins the free 3′-OH of the growing chain, forming a phosphodiester bond
Pyrophosphate (two phosphates) is released

parts.model: A dNTP that base-pairs with the template enters; its 5′ α-phosphate is joined to the 3′-OH at the end of the growing strand by a phosphodiester bond, and pyrophosphate is released.

parts.stem: Which enzyme removes RNA primers in E. coli and replaces them with DNA?

questions.stem: New DNA is made at a replication fork.

parts.stem: Explain why one strand is made continuously and the other in fragments.

scheme.text: DNA polymerase only synthesises 5′→3′
The two template strands are antiparallel
Leading strand made continuously in the direction of fork movement
Lagging strand made discontinuously as Okazaki fragments, each with its own primer, joined by ligase

parts.model: Polymerase only works 5′→3′ and the templates are antiparallel. On one template that direction follows the fork, so the leading strand is made continuously. On the other it runs away from the fork, so the lagging strand is made in short Okazaki fragments, each started by a primer and later joined by DNA ligase.

parts.stem: Name the labelled proteins and structures at the E. coli fork.

questions.stem: State the role of each enzyme in E. coli DNA replication.

parts.stem: (a) Helicase

scheme.text: Unwinds the double helix at the fork

parts.model: Unwinds the helix by breaking the hydrogen bonds between the strands.

parts.stem: (b) DNA gyrase

scheme.text: Removes the supercoiling ahead of the fork (a topoisomerase)

parts.model: Relieves the supercoiling that builds up ahead of the fork.

parts.stem: (c) DNA ligase

scheme.text: Joins Okazaki fragments by sealing the phosphodiester bond

parts.model: Seals the nick between Okazaki fragments with a phosphodiester bond.

parts.stem: (d) DNA polymerase III

scheme.text: Main replicative polymerase: synthesises most of the new DNA

parts.model: The main replicative polymerase, making most of the new DNA.

questions.stem: Replication in E. coli starts at oriC and ends at Ter sites.

parts.stem: Describe oriC and how replication is initiated there.

scheme.text: oriC is 245 bp with three 13 bp repeats and four 9 bp repeats
DnaA proteins (with ATP) bind the 9 bp repeats and the 13 bp (AT-rich) region is denatured
DnaB helicase is loaded (with DnaC) and unwinds, so primase and polymerase can start

parts.model: oriC is 245 bp, with three 13 bp and four 9 bp repeats. About 20 ATP-bound DnaA proteins bind the 9 bp repeats and wrap the DNA, which melts the AT-rich 13 bp repeats. DnaC then loads DnaB helicase onto each strand to unwind the DNA ready for priming.

parts.stem: Explain how replication terminates.

scheme.text: The two forks meet in a terminus region containing Ter sequences
Tus protein binds Ter and arrests a fork approaching from one direction only (fork trap)

parts.model: The two forks, moving in opposite directions from oriC, meet in a terminus region of Ter sequences. Tus bound to Ter lets a fork through from one direction but stops one coming from the other, trapping the forks.

questions.stem: Eukaryotic chromosomes are linear and very long.

parts.stem: Explain how eukaryotes replicate such long DNA quickly.

scheme.text: Many origins of replication are used at once
Each forms a replicon (40–100 kb), replicated bidirectionally, and the bubbles fuse

parts.model: They fire many origins at once. Each replicon (40 to 100 kb) is copied bidirectionally from its origin and neighbouring bubbles fuse.

parts.stem: Explain the end-replication problem and how telomerase solves it.

scheme.text: When the last RNA primer on the lagging strand is removed, the end cannot be filled in
So chromosomes would shorten with every round of replication
Telomerase uses its own RNA template to add repeats to the 3′ end (telomeres)

parts.model: When the final primer on the lagging strand is removed, there is no 3′ end to fill the gap from, so linear chromosomes would shorten each round. Telomerase carries its own RNA template and uses it to add repeats (e.g. TTGGGG) to the 3′ end, which is then completed by normal lagging-strand synthesis.

papers.title: The Genetic Code
papers.hub: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/05 The Genetic Code/The Genetic Code

questions.stem: In the 1960s Brenner predicted that the genetic code is read in triplets.

parts.stem: Explain his reasoning.

scheme.text: 4 bases: singles give 4 combinations and pairs give 16, too few for 20 amino acids
Triplets give 4³ = 64 codons, enough for 20 (with redundancy)

parts.model: With 4 bases, single bases give 4 combinations and pairs only 16, fewer than the 20 amino acids. Triplets give 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 codons, more than enough.

parts.stem: How did Crick's frameshift experiments in phage T4 rII confirm a triplet code?

scheme.text: Inserting or deleting 1 or 2 nucleotides abolished gene function (shifted the reading frame)
Inserting or deleting 3 often restored function
Because three restores the reading frame, the code is read in groups of three

parts.model: Adding or removing one or two nucleotides shifted the reading frame and destroyed rII function, but three insertions (or deletions) often restored it, because three puts the reading frame back in register. So codons are three bases long.

questions.stem: Nirenberg and Matthaei added synthetic RNAs to a cell-free protein-synthesis system and measured radioactive phenylalanine incorporated into protein.

parts.stem: Name the components of the cell-free system.

scheme.text: A synthetic RNA template (e.g. poly-U)
tRNAs with (radioactive) amino acids
Ribosomes
An energy source (GTP)

parts.model: Synthetic mRNA such as poly-U, tRNAs carrying amino acids (one radioactive), ribosomes, and an energy source (GTP).

parts.stem: What do the results show, and how was poly-U made without a DNA template?

scheme.text: Only poly-U gave high radioactivity in protein (about 39,800 counts/min against about 40)
So UUU codes for phenylalanine
Poly-U was made with polynucleotide phosphorylase, which needs no template

parts.model: Poly-U gave about 39,800 counts per minute against about 40 to 50 for poly-A, poly-C or no RNA, so UUU codes for phenylalanine. The RNA was made by polynucleotide phosphorylase, which joins ribonucleotides without a template.

questions.stem: Khorana made repeating copolymers and found which amino acids they coded for.

parts.stem: Repeating UC (UCUCUC…) gave a polypeptide containing leucine and serine. Explain why.

scheme.text: It contains two codons, UCU and CUC, read alternately
One codes leucine and the other serine, alternating in a single polypeptide

parts.model: Repeating UC is read as alternating UCU and CUC codons, so one polypeptide with alternating serine (UCU) and leucine (CUC).

parts.stem: Repeating UUC (UUCUUC…) gave three different polypeptides, each made of one amino acid. Explain why.

scheme.text: It can be read in three frames: UUC, UCU or CUU
Each frame repeats one codon, giving polyPhe, polySer or polyLeu

parts.model: Depending on where reading starts, the message is UUC UUC…, UCU UCU… or CUU CUU…, so three homopolymers: polyphenylalanine, polyserine and polyleucine.

questions.stem: Use the codon table to answer.

parts.stem: Translate this mRNA from its start codon: 5′-GCAUGGCUUCAAAGUGAGC-3′. Give the amino acids (three-letter codes).
parts.model: Met-Ala-Ser-Lys (AUG GCU UCA AAG, then UGA stop)

parts.stem: Explain why a change in the third base of a codon is often silent.

scheme.text: The code is redundant: most amino acids have several codons
Synonymous codons usually differ only at the third base (wobble), so the amino acid is unchanged

parts.model: 61 codons code for 20 amino acids, so most have several codons, and these usually differ only in the third base. Changing it often gives a codon for the same amino acid.

questions.stem: Features of the genetic code.

parts.stem: Which three codons are stop codons?
Explain what "non-overlapping" and "commaless" mean.

scheme.text: Non-overlapping: each nucleotide is part of only one codon
Commaless: codons follow one another with no gaps or spacers

parts.model: Non-overlapping: each nucleotide belongs to one codon only. Commaless: codons are read one after another with no gaps or spacer bases between them.

parts.stem: State the wobble hypothesis.

scheme.text: The first two codon bases pair strictly with the anticodon
The third position pairs less strictly, so one tRNA can read more than one codon

parts.model: The first two bases of a codon pair strictly with the anticodon, but pairing at the third position is looser, so one tRNA can read more than one codon.

parts.stem: Why is the code described as only "nearly" universal?

scheme.text: In some species UGA codes for selenocysteine
In some species UAG codes for pyrrolysine

parts.model: In some proteins of some species, the stop codons are read differently: UGA as selenocysteine and UAG as pyrrolysine.

questions.stem: Part of a gene's coding strand reads 5′-ATGGCCAAGTGGTAA-3′.

parts.stem: Write the mRNA transcribed from this gene, 5′ to 3′.
parts.model: 5′-AUGGCCAAGUGGUAA-3′
parts.note: The mRNA has the same sequence as the coding strand, with U for T.

parts.stem: Give the peptide it encodes (three-letter codes).
parts.model: Met-Ala-Lys-Trp, then UAA stop

parts.stem: Which strand does RNA polymerase read, and in which direction is the RNA made?

scheme.text: It reads the template (non-coding) strand, 3′→5′
RNA is made 5′→3′

parts.model: RNA polymerase reads the template strand 3′→5′ and builds the RNA 5′→3′.

questions.stem: The figure shows a typical E. coli promoter.

parts.stem: Fill in the consensus sequences and spacings.
What is the role of the sigma factor?

scheme.text: It recognises and binds the −10 and −35 boxes of the promoter
So RNA polymerase starts at the right place; it leaves once elongation begins; different sigmas switch on different genes

parts.model: σ binds the −35 and −10 boxes so the RNA polymerase core starts at the right place, then leaves as the chain grows. Different σ factors recognise different sets of promoters.

parts.stem: Distinguish intrinsic and extrinsic termination.

scheme.text: Intrinsic: a GC-rich hairpin in the RNA (followed by Us) releases polymerase and RNA
Extrinsic: needs the rho protein

parts.model: Intrinsic terminators form an RNA hairpin that makes the polymerase release the RNA. Extrinsic (rho-dependent) termination needs the rho protein.

questions.stem: The lac operon is controlled by lactose and by glucose.

parts.stem: (a) Glucose present, lactose absent. State the level of transcription and explain it.

scheme.text: Off / no transcription
The repressor (from lacI) is bound to the operator, blocking RNA polymerase

parts.model: Off: with no lactose, the lacI repressor sits on the operator and blocks RNA polymerase.

parts.stem: (b) Glucose present, lactose present.

scheme.text: Low
Repressor released by lactose (allolactose), but cAMP is low so CAP does not activate

parts.model: Low: lactose (allolactose) releases the repressor, but glucose keeps cAMP low so CAP–cAMP does not bind and activation is weak.

parts.stem: (c) Glucose absent, lactose present.

scheme.text: High
Repressor released and cAMP–CAP binds the CAP site, activating transcription

parts.model: High: the repressor is released, and with no glucose cAMP rises; cAMP–CAP binds next to the promoter and strongly activates transcription.

parts.stem: (d) A lacI mutant whose repressor cannot bind the operator, with no lactose. Explain the result.

scheme.text: Constitutive expression (always on)
The repressor cannot block the operator
kw: cannot|can.t|unable|not bind|no longer|never|doesn.t bind|does not bind

parts.model: Constitutive expression: the faulty repressor never sits on the operator, so the genes are transcribed even without lactose.

parts.stem: (e) An Iˢ mutant whose repressor cannot bind lactose, with lactose present.

scheme.text: Repressed / never induced (stays off)
The repressor stays on the operator because lactose cannot release it

parts.model: Repressed: lactose cannot bind the repressor, so it never leaves the operator and the operon stays off.

questions.stem: Eukaryotic transcription and RNA processing.

parts.stem: Describe how transcription by RNA polymerase II is initiated.

scheme.text: Chromatin remodelling (e.g. SWI–SNF) exposes the promoter
TBP binds the TATA box; TAFs help Pol II bind, forming the basal transcription complex
Transcription factors at enhancers increase initiation (up to about 100×)

parts.model: Chromatin remodelling complexes such as SWI–SNF expose the promoter. TBP binds the TATA box, and TBP-associated factors help RNA Pol II bind, forming the basal transcription complex. Transcription factors bound at enhancers raise initiation up to about 100-fold.

parts.stem: Describe the processing that turns a primary transcript into mature mRNA.

scheme.text: 5′ cap: a G added by a 5′–5′ triphosphate link, then methylated
3′ end cut downstream of AAUAAA
Poly-A polymerase adds 100–200 A (poly-A tail)
Splicing removes introns and joins exons
By the spliceosome (snRNPs) at the splice donor, branch site and acceptor

parts.model: A G is added to the 5′ end through a 5′–5′ triphosphate link and methylated (the cap). The 3′ end is cut downstream of AAUAAA and poly-A polymerase adds 100 to 200 A. The spliceosome, using snRNPs that pair with the splice donor, branch site and acceptor, cuts out the introns as lariats and joins the exons.

parts.stem: Explain why alternative splicing matters.

scheme.text: Exons can be joined in different combinations
So one gene gives several mRNAs and proteins, increasing protein diversity

parts.model: Joining exons in different combinations lets one gene make several mRNAs and proteins, increasing protein diversity without more genes.

questions.stem: The diagram shows a ribosome.

parts.stem: Name the labelled sites and subunits.
State what occupies each of the A, P and E sites during elongation.

scheme.text: A site: incoming aminoacyl (charged) tRNA
P site: peptidyl-tRNA carrying the growing chain
E site: uncharged tRNA about to leave

parts.model: A site: the incoming aminoacyl-tRNA. P site: the peptidyl-tRNA holding the growing chain. E site: the uncharged tRNA about to leave.

questions.stem: tRNAs must be charged before translation.

parts.stem: Describe how a tRNA is charged.

scheme.text: An aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase specific to the amino acid
Uses ATP to activate the amino acid (aminoacyl-AMP)
Attaches the amino acid to the 3′ end of the matching tRNA

parts.model: An aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase uses ATP to activate the amino acid as aminoacyl-AMP, then transfers it to the 3′ end of the matching tRNA, making an aminoacyl (charged) tRNA.

parts.stem: What is the minimum number of different tRNAs needed to read all 61 sense codons?
Explain why fewer than 61 tRNAs are needed.

scheme.text: Wobble at the third codon position lets one tRNA read more than one codon

parts.model: Wobble pairing at the third codon position lets one tRNA read several codons.

questions.stem: Translation in bacteria.

parts.stem: Describe initiation of translation in bacteria.

scheme.text: Initiation factors and mRNA bind the small (30S) subunit
The Shine–Dalgarno sequence (AGGAGG) pairs with 16S rRNA, positioning AUG
IF2 (with GTP) brings fMet-tRNA, whose UAC anticodon pairs with AUG in the P site
The 50S subunit joins and the initiation factors leave

parts.model: IF1 and IF3 bind the 30S subunit, which binds the mRNA when its Shine–Dalgarno sequence (AGGAGG) pairs with 16S rRNA, placing AUG in position. IF2–GTP brings fMet-tRNA, whose UAC anticodon pairs with AUG in the P site. The 50S subunit then joins, and IF1 and IF2 leave.

parts.stem: Describe one cycle of elongation.

scheme.text: EF-Tu (with GTP) brings a charged tRNA to the A site, matching codon and anticodon
Peptidyl transferase forms a peptide bond, moving the chain onto the A-site tRNA
This is catalysed by the 23S rRNA (the ribosome is a ribozyme)
EF-G moves the ribosome one codon (3 nt); P-site tRNA to E and exits, A-site tRNA to P

parts.model: EF-Tu–GTP delivers a charged tRNA to the A site, where it is accepted if its anticodon matches the codon. Peptidyl transferase activity of the 23S rRNA joins the chain to the new amino acid. EF-G then moves the ribosome one codon along: the empty tRNA moves from P to E and leaves, and the peptidyl-tRNA moves from A to P.

parts.stem: At about 15 amino acids per second, how many seconds does a ribosome take to make a 300-amino-acid protein?

questions.stem: Codons and anticodons pair antiparallel.

parts.stem: Write the anticodon (5′ to 3′) of the tRNA that reads the codon 5′-GCA-3′.
parts.model: 5′-UGC-3′ (it pairs as 3′-CGU-5′)
parts.note: CGU is the right bases written 3′→5′.

parts.stem: Describe how translation is terminated.

scheme.text: A stop codon (UAA, UAG or UGA) enters the A site; no tRNA matches it
A release factor binds: RF1 reads UAA/UAG and RF2 reads UAA/UGA
Hydrolysis frees the polypeptide from the P-site tRNA; the ribosome dissociates

parts.model: When a stop codon reaches the A site, a release factor binds instead of a tRNA (RF1 for UAA or UAG, RF2 for UAA or UGA). It triggers hydrolysis of the bond between the polypeptide and the P-site tRNA, releasing the chain, and the ribosome comes apart.

parts.stem: What is a polyribosome, and what is its advantage?

scheme.text: Several ribosomes translating one mRNA at the same time
Many copies of the protein are made quickly from one mRNA

parts.model: Several ribosomes translating the same mRNA at once, so many copies of the protein are made quickly from one message.

papers.title: Plasmids and Recombinant DNA
papers.hub: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/08 Plasmids and Recombinant DNA/Plasmids and Recombinant DNA (Lecture 8)

questions.stem: Restriction enzymes are central to recombinant DNA technology.

parts.stem: What does a restriction enzyme do, and what is special about its recognition site?

scheme.text: Binds a specific short DNA sequence (recognition site)
Cuts the phosphodiester backbone on both strands
The site is usually palindromic (4 or 6 bp), reading the same 5′→3′ on both strands

parts.model: It binds a specific short sequence, its recognition site, and cuts the phosphodiester backbone of both strands there. Sites are usually 4 or 6 bp and palindromic: the same reading 5′→3′ on each strand.

parts.stem: On average, how many base pairs apart will a 6-base recognition site occur in random DNA?
How many EcoRI sites (GAATTC) are in 5′-TTGAATTCAGCGATGAATTCTA-3′?
Explain the difference between sticky and blunt ends, giving one enzyme that makes each.

scheme.text: Sticky ends: single-stranded overhangs from offset (staggered) cuts
Blunt ends: both strands cut at the same point, no overhang
e.g. EcoRI/HindIII/BamHI sticky; AluI blunt

parts.model: Sticky (cohesive) ends have short single-stranded overhangs made by staggered cuts, e.g. EcoRI (G^AATTC). Blunt ends have none, because both strands are cut at the same point, e.g. AluI (AG^CT).

questions.stem: Plasmid vectors carry DNA into bacteria.

parts.stem: List four properties of a good cloning vector.

scheme.text: Several unique restriction sites (a multiple cloning site)
Replicates independently in the host (has an origin of replication)
A selectable marker, e.g. antibiotic resistance
Easy to isolate / recover from the host
Small, or a reporter gene such as lacZ

parts.model: Several unique restriction sites for inserting DNA; its own origin so it replicates independently; a selectable marker such as ampicillin resistance; and easy isolation from the host cell.

parts.stem: Name the features of pUC18.
Explain how blue-white screening identifies bacteria carrying recombinant pUC18.

scheme.text: Plates contain ampicillin, so only cells that took up a plasmid grow
The polylinker lies inside lacZ, so an insert disrupts lacZ
Without working β-galactosidase, X-gal is not cleaved, so recombinant colonies are white
Colonies with no insert make β-galactosidase, cleave X-gal and turn blue

parts.model: The plates hold ampicillin, so only cells with a plasmid grow. The polylinker sits inside lacZ, so an insert disrupts the gene: no β-galactosidase is made, X-gal is not cut, and the colony stays white. Plasmids without an insert make β-galactosidase, which cleaves X-gal to a blue product.

questions.stem: Cloning a gene into a plasmid.

parts.stem: Describe the steps used to clone a DNA fragment into a plasmid and recover cells carrying it.

scheme.text: Cut vector and insert DNA with the same restriction enzyme
Sticky ends anneal and DNA ligase seals the nicks (phosphodiester bonds)
Introduce into bacteria by transformation (CaCl₂ + heat shock, or electroporation)
Select on antibiotic / screen (e.g. X-gal) for recombinant colonies

parts.model: Cut the plasmid and the DNA to be cloned with the same restriction enzyme so their sticky ends match; mix so the ends anneal, and seal the nicks with DNA ligase; transform bacteria (calcium chloride and heat shock, or electroporation); then plate on antibiotic (and X-gal) to select and identify recombinant colonies.

parts.stem: Give the natural role of restriction enzymes and of DNA ligase in cells.

scheme.text: Restriction enzymes: bacterial defence (innate immunity) against bacteriophage DNA
Ligase: seals breaks in replication (Okazaki fragments), repair and recombination

parts.model: Restriction enzymes protect bacteria by cutting the DNA of invading phages (the host methylates its own sites). DNA ligase seals breaks during replication (joining Okazaki fragments), repair and recombination.

questions.stem: A linear 10.0 kb fragment was cut with EcoRI, with BamHI, and with both. The fragments were separated on a gel.

parts.stem: How many kb apart are the EcoRI and BamHI sites?
parts.working: EcoRI is 3.0 kb from one end and BamHI 4.0 kb (or 6.0 kb) from an end. The double digest 3.0 + 1.0 + 6.0 only fits BamHI 4.0 kb from the same end, so the sites are 1.0 kb apart.

parts.stem: Explain why the double digest is needed to place the sites.

scheme.text: Single digests only give each site's distance from an end, not which end
The double digest shows how the two sites lie relative to each other

parts.model: A single digest tells you how far each site is from an end but not from which end. Only the double digest shows the sites' positions relative to each other.

parts.stem: Which fragments travel furthest through the gel, and why?

scheme.text: The smallest fragments
DNA is negatively charged and moves to the positive electrode; small fragments pass through the agarose mesh more easily

parts.model: The smallest. DNA's phosphates make it negative, so it moves towards the positive electrode, and small fragments get through the gel's mesh fastest.

papers.title: Polymerase Chain Reaction
papers.hub: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Lectures/10 Polymerase Chain Reaction/Polymerase Chain Reaction (Lecture 10)

questions.stem: PCR amplifies a chosen region of DNA.

parts.stem: List the five components needed to set up a PCR.

scheme.text: Template DNA
Two primers (~20 nt oligonucleotides)
dNTPs (dATP, dCTP, dGTP, dTTP)
Buffer with Mg²⁺
A thermostable DNA polymerase such as Taq

parts.model: Template DNA, two primers of about 20 nucleotides, the four dNTPs, a buffer containing Mg²⁺, and a thermostable DNA polymerase such as Taq.

parts.stem: Describe the three steps of one PCR cycle, with temperatures.

scheme.text: Denaturation at 92–95 °C separates the strands
Annealing at 50–65 °C: primers bind the complementary sequences
Extension at about 72 °C: polymerase extends the primers' 3′ ends

parts.model: Denature at 92 to 95 °C to separate the strands; anneal at 50 to 65 °C so the primers bind; extend at about 72 °C as the polymerase adds nucleotides to each primer's 3′ end.

parts.stem: Why must the polymerase be thermostable?

scheme.text: Each cycle heats to ~95 °C, which would denature an ordinary polymerase
A thermostable enzyme (Taq, from Thermus aquaticus) survives, so it need not be re-added each cycle

parts.model: Every cycle heats the reaction to about 95 °C, which would denature most enzymes. Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus survives, so it does not have to be added again after each cycle.

questions.stem: Designing primers for the PCR.

parts.stem: Calculate Tm for the primer 5′-AGCTTGCAGGCATCGAATCG-3′ using Tm = (4 × GC) + (2 × AT).
What annealing temperature would you use?
Give two rules for designing a pair of PCR primers.

scheme.text: 3′ ends point towards each other, one primer on each strand
About 20 nt long, complementary to the flanking sequences
Usually 500–5000 nt apart, with similar Tm

parts.model: The primers bind opposite strands with their 3′ ends pointing towards each other across the target, typically 500 to 5000 nucleotides apart; each is about 20 nucleotides, complementary to a flanking sequence, with similar Tm.

questions.stem: The number of copies grows each cycle.

parts.stem: Starting from 100 copies of a target, how many copies are there after 30 perfect cycles? (Give your answer like 1.07e11.)
Explain why the real increase is less than double per cycle in later cycles.

scheme.text: Reagents (primers, dNTPs) run low
Polymerase loses activity / product strands re-anneal, so not every molecule is copied

parts.model: Primers and dNTPs are used up, the polymerase gradually loses activity and product strands re-anneal to each other, so not every molecule is copied each cycle.

parts.stem: A lab can use Taq or a high-fidelity polymerase. Which would you choose to clone a gene for protein expression, and why?

scheme.text: High-fidelity polymerase
Fewer errors, so the cloned sequence (and protein) is correct; accepting slower/dearer

parts.model: A high-fidelity (proofreading) polymerase: it makes far fewer errors, so the cloned gene encodes the correct protein, even though it is slower and more expensive.

questions.stem: PCR can also start from RNA and can be measured as it runs.

parts.stem: Explain how PCR can be used to measure the expression of a gene.

scheme.text: RNA is copied into cDNA by reverse transcriptase (RT-PCR)
Real-time (quantitative) PCR measures the product each cycle by fluorescence
More starting template (higher expression) gives a signal that rises in fewer cycles

parts.model: Reverse transcriptase copies the mRNA into cDNA, which is then amplified (RT-PCR). In real-time PCR a fluorescent dye or probe reports the amount of product after each cycle; a sample with more starting mRNA (higher expression) reaches the detectable signal in fewer cycles.

parts.stem: Which is not a use of PCR described in the lecture?
options: Amplifying a gene to clone into an expression vector
Amplifying DNA before sequencing for diagnosis
parts.explain: Cutting DNA at specific sequences is what restriction enzymes do.

papers.title: Practicals
papers.hub: 01 Year 1/Molecular Biology and Genetics/Molecular Biology and Genetics

questions.stem: Practical 1. A standard curve of absorbance at 260 nm against DNA concentration had the equation A = 0.020C + 0.005 (C in µg/mL, R² = 0.996). The unknown was diluted by adding 50 µL to 950 µL of TE buffer, and the diluted sample read A = 0.245.

parts.stem: Calculate the DNA concentration of the diluted sample.
Calculate the concentration of the original undiluted sample.
parts.working: 50 µL in 1000 µL is a 1 in 20 dilution: 12 × 20 = 240 µg/mL.

parts.stem: What does R² = 0.996 tell you?

scheme.text: The data fit the straight line very closely (strongly linear)

parts.model: The points lie very close to the straight line: a strong linear fit.

parts.stem: Why is the spectrophotometer zeroed with a tube of buffer only, and what do Tris and EDTA do in TE buffer?

scheme.text: The buffer-only blank removes the background absorbance of the buffer and cuvette
Tris keeps the pH stable
EDTA binds metal ions that DNA-degrading enzymes need, protecting the DNA

parts.model: The blank contains everything except DNA, so zeroing on it removes the background absorbance. Tris keeps the pH stable; EDTA binds the metal ions (e.g. Mg²⁺) that DNA-degrading enzymes need.

questions.stem: Practical 2. A 5000 bp circular plasmid was cut with enzymes X, Y and Z. X is placed at position 0.

parts.stem: Each single digest gave one 5000 bp fragment. How many sites does each enzyme have?
parts.working: Cutting a circle once just opens it into one linear fragment.

parts.stem: From the X + Y and X + Z digests, Y is at 1500. Use the Y + Z digest to give the position of Z (in bp from X, going the same way round).
parts.working: X + Z puts Z at 2000 or 3000. Y + Z = 500 + 4500 means Y and Z are 500 bp apart, so Z is at 2000 (at 3000 it would be 1500 bp from Y).

parts.stem: Predict the fragments from the triple digest X + Y + Z.

scheme.text: 1500 bp (X to Y) and 500 bp (Y to Z)
3000 bp (Z back to X)

questions.stem: Practical 3. E. coli HB101 was transformed with pBR322. 100 µL samples were spread on plates. The 10⁻⁶ dilution of the starting cells gave 45 colonies on LB agar. The undiluted transformation mix gave 120 colonies on LB + ampicillin.

parts.stem: Calculate the total number of viable cells per mL (CFU/mL). (Give answers like 4.5e8.)
Calculate the transformed cells per mL.
Calculate the frequency of transformation.
Explain why the cells recover in LB broth at 37 °C before plating on ampicillin, and why untransformed cells are also plated on ampicillin.

scheme.text: Recovery lets the ampicillin-resistance (bla) gene be expressed before the cells meet the antibiotic
The control shows the cells were not already resistant, so growth on the test plate is due to the plasmid

parts.model: Recovery gives transformed cells time to express the plasmid's ampicillin-resistance gene before meeting the antibiotic. Untransformed cells on ampicillin should not grow, confirming that any growth on the test plate comes from the plasmid.
